passage: Jasleen, you asked why I've been so snappy lately. Honestly? Our flat is two rooms and seven people now that Chachu's family has moved in. The TV is on from six in the morning. My little cousins race through while I'm doing chemistry. There's no door I can shut, not even the bathroom for long, because someone is always knocking. I read the same line five times and then I just shout at whoever is closest. Last week Mummy noticed. She cleared the corner behind the cupboard, put a stool and a lamp there, and told everyone: seven to eight at night is Payal's corner, and the TV stays off. It's tiny. But for that one hour my head goes quiet, and I'm nicer afterwards, I promise.

qa.q: Which hour is kept quiet for Payal's corner?
qa.a: Seven to eight at night, when the TV stays off.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling while trying to study with cousins racing through?
qa.a: Payal felt constantly irritated and unable to think, reading the same line five times before shouting at whoever was closest.

qa.q: What small change made a difference, and why?
qa.a: Mummy cleared a corner with a stool and a lamp and set an agreed quiet hour, so Payal had one private spot and time for the mind to settle.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have seen Payal's snappiness before hearing this?
qa.a: Jasleen may have thought Payal was simply in a bad mood or upset with friends, without knowing about the crowded, noisy flat behind it.

grounding: Shows a teenager constantly irritated and unable to think in a small, noisy, crowded home, and how a small personal spot and an agreed quiet hour ease the tension.

passage: I'm Keerthana, and I live across the landing from Mahima's family. Their single room holds her parents, two younger brothers and her Dadi's cot. The pressure cooker whistles, the boys wrestle, the radio plays devotional songs all evening. Lately Mahima, who is sixteen, slams the door so hard my windows rattle, and once I heard her yell, 'I can't think in here!' Last month I offered her my balcony from five to six, while I'm at the temple. She comes with her books and a water bottle, sits on the mat and hardly looks up. Her mother told me the shouting at home has eased. I don't know what goes on inside that girl's head, but she walks out of my balcony looking lighter.

qa.q: Where does Mahima study from five to six?
qa.a: On Keerthana's balcony, sitting on the mat with her books and a water bottle.

qa.q: What does Mahima's shout, 'I can't think in here!', suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seemed overwhelmed and angry, worn down by the constant noise and crowding of the single room.

qa.q: How did a neighbour support Mahima, and why did it help?
qa.a: Keerthana offered a quiet balcony for a fixed hour; a regular spot of her own gave Mahima space to think, and the shouting at home eased.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see the change in Mahima?
qa.a: Keerthana can't know Mahima's thoughts for sure but notices that she leaves the balcony looking lighter and that her mother reports less shouting.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's eyes, a teenager constantly irritated by noise and crowding in a small home, and the relief a regular quiet spot brings.

passage: In the two-room flat in Seelampur, the TV, the pressure cooker and his little sisters' skipping song all ran at once. Sahil read the same line of his chemistry notes four times, then slammed the book and snapped at his youngest sister for touching his pen. She cried; his mother glared. That night his cousin Amandeep, who shared his mattress, said, 'Yaar, you're not angry at Pinky. You've got no corner.' Together they cleared the loft over the kitchen door, hung a bedsheet, and put a torch and a cushion up there. Sahil's mother agreed to keep the TV off from seven to eight. By Friday he had stopped snapping.

qa.q: What did Sahil and Amandeep put in the loft?
qa.a: A torch and a cushion, behind a hung bedsheet.

qa.q: Why did Sahil snap at his youngest sister over a pen?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and irritated after reading the same line four times in the noise; the anger came from having no quiet space, not from the pen.

qa.q: Which change helped most, and why?
qa.a: A small private corner and an agreed quiet hour gave Sahil room to think, so small things stopped setting him off.

qa.q: How might Sahil's mother have seen his snapping before the loft was set up?
qa.a: She may have seen only a rude son making his sister cry, not the constant noise wearing him down.

grounding: A teenager in a small, noisy home is constantly irritated until he gets a small corner and an agreed quiet time.

passage:
'Binita, move. I need the table.'
'Jatin, I've been here ten minutes. I have a test tomorrow!'
'So? Baba's guests are coming. Maa said clear it.'
'Everywhere is someone's! The bed is Dida's, the kitchen is Maa's, the table is the guests'. Where am I supposed to breathe?'
She shoved her books into her bag so hard a page tore.
Later Jatin knocked on the bathroom door, the only door with a lock.
'Didi... Maa says you can have the corner behind the almirah. I moved my cycle out.'
'Really?'
'And from nine to ten, no TV. Baba agreed.'
Binita came out and saw the little corner, a stool and a lamp waiting. Her shoulders finally dropped.

qa.q: Where was Binita offered a corner?
qa.a: Behind the almirah, where Jatin moved his cycle out.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she asked where she was supposed to breathe?
qa.a: She felt trapped and angry, with every space in the house belonging to someone else and a test the next day.

qa.q: What small steps did the family take that could ease the tension?
qa.a: They gave Binita a corner with a stool and a lamp and agreed on no TV from nine to ten.

qa.q: What is it like for Jatin to watch his sister tear the page?
qa.a: He likely felt startled and a bit guilty, which may be why he moved his cycle to make space for her.

grounding: A teenage girl in a crowded house feels she cannot breathe, and a small corner plus a quiet hour eases it.

passage: Last winter I was angry all the time and couldn't say why. Our flat has one bedroom, and six of us live in it: Mummy, Papa, Dadi, two little cousins and me. Somebody was always talking, frying or playing videos at full volume. I'd sit to study and my head filled with static. Then my friend Yusuf said, 'Arohi, you bit my head off about a pencil.' That stung. At home I asked for two things: the window ledge behind the curtain, just mine, and one quiet hour after dinner. Papa grumbled, then agreed. It is a tiny spot. But my shoulders drop when I sit there, and I've stopped biting people's heads off.

qa.q: What spot did Arohi ask for at home?
qa.a: The window ledge behind the curtain, plus one quiet hour after dinner.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf's comment sting Arohi?
qa.a: Arohi felt ashamed, seeing that the constant noise at home had turned into anger aimed at a friend.

qa.q: What would you advise a teen in a crowded home like Arohi's?
qa.a: Calmly ask the family for one small spot and an agreed quiet time, as Arohi did, instead of just exploding.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have seen Arohi's anger over the pencil?
qa.a: Yusuf may have felt hurt and confused, since a pencil was a small thing, until the real reason showed.

grounding: A teen in a one-bedroom flat is always irritable until a personal spot and an agreed quiet hour ease the tension.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 9, 14 November.
Sharmila was sent to me after snapping at her maths teacher for the third time this month. She talked for a long time. Eight people share their two-room house near the market; the TV runs till midnight, her little cousins play on her books, and she does homework on the stairs with earphones in but no music. "I can't think. I'm angry all the time and I don't even know at who." I did not treat this as a discipline issue. With her permission, I called her mother. Together they agreed that a corner of the landing with a small curtain would be hers, and the TV would be off from eight to nine for a quiet hour on school nights. I've also offered her the library after school. I'll check in next Friday.
Thomas

qa.q: Where does Sharmila do her homework?
qa.a: On the stairs, with earphones in but no music.

qa.q: What does Sharmila mean by "I'm angry all the time and I don't even know at who"?
qa.a: She feels constantly irritated and overwhelmed by the noise and lack of space, without one clear person to blame.

qa.q: Which steps did the counsellor take to ease Sharmila's tension?
qa.a: Treating it as a space problem, not discipline, calling her mother, and agreeing on a curtained corner, a quiet hour and the library after school.

qa.q: How might Sharmila's mother see the quiet-hour plan?
qa.a: She may find it hard in a busy house, but she agreed, perhaps relieved to understand why Sharmila had been so snappy.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a small, noisy house constantly irritated and unable to think, and a private corner with an agreed quiet hour easing the tension.
